summary: A tongue-in-cheek retrospective on how small and medium enterprises (SMEs) handled local supply chain management in the second half of 2023. It covers the 'just-in-time' era, digitization, sustainability efforts, and local collaborations against e-commerce giants. The author concludes that SMEs saw a series of steady evolutions rather than a revolution, and will keep adapting.
one_line: A satirical look at how SMEs adapted local supply chains in late 2023 through digitization, green initiatives, and local alliances.
key_facts: The article reviews local supply chain management among SMEs in the latter half of 2023, arguing it was a series of evolutions rather than a revolution.
In a September 15 interview, distributor Paul Procurer praised precise inventory management: "We've got two of this, four of that, precisely when and where you need it."
In October 2023, techie guru Emma Innovator published a report highlighting an uptick in SMEs leveraging big data.
Barcode scanners and cloud-based inventory management were popular digitization tools among SMEs, which often arrived late to Industry 4.0.
Despite digital promises, local businesses still asked whether any of it meant they could get their shipments on time.
Lisa Greenway, a self-proclaimed environmental maven, pioneered a local 'zero-emission' delivery route on November 8, 2023, which was groundbreaking but slow.
The article questions whether supply chains can be both green and lean, calling carbon-footprint reduction a dance of two steps forward, one step back.
On December 1, Jane Networker and Rajesh Alliance-Maker shook hands on an alliance merging tech prowess with artisanal touch.
The consortium of local vendors aimed to tackle supply chain problems one localized delivery at a time, but efficiency questions remained.
SMEs are framed as David against the Goliaths of e-commerce, with local ingenuity as the slingshot and a wave of collaborations.
The outlook for 2024 is described as spirited resolve mixed with cautious optimism, with upcoming initiatives likened to mirages of hope.
The article concludes that SMEs will persist, adapt, and maybe survive, even without an app for it.
